title: Giant Bulrush: How to Spot and Control Tikiw in Your Rice Field
metaTitle: Giant Bulrush in Rice: How to Spot and Control Tikiw
metaDescription: Giant bulrush, known as tikiw, is a tall sedge in lowland rice fields. Learn how to spot it and how to dig out its rootstocks so it stays gone for good.
excerpt: Giant bulrush, or Scirpus grossus, is a large sedge weed of irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. Farmers know it as tikiw. It spreads by seed and by rootstocks under the soil. This page shows how to spot it in your palay and how to control it so it does not come back.

heroImage.alt: Giant bulrush (Scirpus grossus), a sedge weed of Philippine rice fields
heroImage.credit: Wibowo Djatmiko (Wie146), CC BY SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
This damo is a sedge from the Cyperaceae family. Filipino farmers call it tikiw. As its English name says, giant bulrush is a big, tall sedge. It shows up in both irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields, where it can stand above the palay around it.

Some plants live for one season only, while others keep growing as perennials. It spreads by seed and by rootstocks, which are thick underground stems at the base of the plant. Seeds drop into the soil and sprout with the next crop. Meanwhile, a rootstock left in the mud can send up new shoots after you cut the top. So pulling the leaves alone rarely ends the problem. You need to take out what lies below the soil as well.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about giant bulrush
rows: Irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields

blocks.text: Like all sedges, it has a solid, triangular stem with no nodes. Roll the stem between your fingers and you will feel three clear edges. This plant grows tall and stout, so you can often spot it above the rice. At the top it carries many brown spikelets, each one egg shaped. Rice, on the other hand, has a round, hollow stem with joints.

items: A thick, three sided stem that feels solid and has no joints.
Tall plants standing out above the palay canopy.
Many brown, egg shaped spikelets crowded at the top of the stem.
New shoots rising from the same spot after cutting, a sign of living rootstocks.

blocks.text:
Like most sedges, giant bulrush competes with palay for light, water and fertilizer. Because it grows so big, it can shade the rice around it and take a large share of the nutrients. Where it forms clumps, fewer rice plants can grow in that space.

When it flowers, its seeds can mix with harvested palay and lower the quality of seed you keep. Plants that survive as perennials also come back crop after crop. Dense clumps give rats and insect pests a place to hide close to the rice hills.

items: Dig out each clump with its rootstocks, using a spade or bolo, because cut stems sprout again from what stays in the mud.
Remove young plants early, while they are small and their rootstocks are still easy to pull.
Cut and remove plants before the brown spikelets ripen, so they do not add seed to the field.
Clear tikiw from canals and field edges too, since clumps there can spread back into the paddy.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Sedges

If water and weeding cannot hold giant bulrush down, choose an active ingredient that works on sedges at the age of your rice. The table follows PhilRice recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Giant Bulrush Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Plow and harrow well, and rake out the runners, roots or pieces you turn up. A small piece left in wet soil can grow a new plant.
Pull escapes before their flower clusters turn brown, since one clump drops a great deal of tiny seed.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [sedge weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.
Not Sure It Is Giant Bulrush?

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. Anee tells you which weed it most likely is, its group, and what to do at the age of your rice. blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Giant Bulrush

items.q: What do Filipino farmers call giant bulrush?
items.a: Filipino farmers call it tikiw. Its scientific name is Scirpus grossus, and it belongs to the sedge family, Cyperaceae. If you are unsure, look for a tall plant with a thick, triangular stem and many brown, egg shaped spikelets at the top. Those traits set it apart from rice and from smaller sedges.

items.q: How do I control it in my rice field?
items.a: Use clean seed and keep the field level with steady water. Then dig out young plants early, rootstocks and all, before they flower. Clear clumps from canals and bunds as well. If you need a herbicide, choose one that works on sedges and fits the age of your rice. Always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Why does tikiw keep coming back after I cut it?
items.a: It comes back because cutting leaves the rootstocks alive under the soil. Those rootstocks send up new shoots, and some plants keep growing as perennials. Seeds dropped earlier can also sprout with the next crop. So dig out whole clumps with their rootstocks, and remove plants before they flower.
